_: المرحلة 20-3 — which composite index each 20-2 keyset page rides.
One row per keysetWhere(...) call site, keyed by <file>#<function>. `index`
names a b-tree whose columns END in (column, id); `keyset-index.guard.mjs`
reads the CREATE INDEX out of prisma/migrations — not out of schema.prisma —
so a declaration nobody ever migrated cannot pass as coverage.
`index: null` means «an existing index already serves this page, measured».
It requires a reason carrying the two numbers, and the count of them may only
FALL. Numbers below are median-of-five EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the
half way down each list. Re-measure with `pnpm perf:evidence`.

lists.reason: Ordered by (sku, id), and `products_store_sku_live_key` is UNIQUE on (store_id, sku) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL — the same LIVE predicate this list carries. A unique key means sku already identifies the row, so the id tiebreaker can never break a tie and an index carrying it would be dead weight. Measured 0.116 ms on 40,000 live products in one store.

Same shape as the products list beside it: `store_orders_store_id_order_number_key` is UNIQUE on (store_id, order_number), so order_number alone orders the store's rows and the id tiebreaker is unreachable. Measured 0.139 ms on 100,000 orders in one store.

`order_notes_store_order_idx` is (store_id, order_id, created_at) and stops before id, so the plan carries an Incremental Sort — but that sort runs inside created_at TIES, which are single rows, so it does not grow with the thread. Measured 0.058 ms on an order carrying 20,001 notes; the (…, id) variant was not worth replacing a live index for.

`inventory_reservations_pending_inspection_idx` is (store_id, returned_at DESC) WHERE return_disposition = 'pending_inspection' — the exact predicate this list carries — and stops before id. Measured 0.09 ms; the (…, id DESC) variant measured 0.08 ms, which does not buy the churn of replacing a live index. The residual Incremental Sort is over returned_at ties only.

One keyset over FOUR tables (products, product_categories, coupons, store_staff_memberships), each carrying `*_store_trash_idx` as (store_id, deleted_at DESC) WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL — the predicate the trash bin always applies — stopping before id. Measured 0.13 ms on 10,000 trashed products against 0.05 ms for the (…, id DESC) variant: real, but 0.08 ms, and the residual Incremental Sort is over deleted_at ties, so it does not grow with the bin. Four live indexes is too much churn for that.
